analysis.one_liner: Requires mortgage companies to evaluate homeowners for loan modifications before foreclosing, caps foreclosure fees, and funds mediation programs.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Financial Services Committee and its subcommittees until the two-year Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have stopped mortgage companies from starting or continuing a foreclosure unless they first checked whether the homeowner qualified for a loan modification that costs the company less than foreclosing, and handed over documents like the payment history and proof they even own the loan. It also barred most fees charged during the modification process, voided any foreclosure sale done in violation of these rules, gave states grants to run free foreclosure mediation programs, and moved $1 billion from bank bailout warrant proceeds into a Housing Trust Fund for affordable housing.
analysis.who_benefits: Homeowners in financial hardship facing foreclosure on their primary residence: the bill would have forced mortgage companies to prove they reviewed the case for a modification, disclose the paperwork behind a foreclosure, suspend foreclosure deadlines for loans already in process, and void sales done without compliance. State and local governments would have received grants to run free mediation programs, and affordable housing builders would benefit from the $1 billion Housing Trust Fund transfer.

how_it_helps.text: A mortgage company could not start a judicial or nonjudicial foreclosure until it made its best effort to determine whether the homeowner qualifies for a loan modification that yields more money than foreclosing, and to offer one if so.

Homeowners deemed ineligible must be given documentation of the modification and net-present-value calculations, the loan origination including proof the company has the right to foreclose, any pooling and servicing agreement, their payment history, and the foreclosure alternatives considered — tools to catch robo-signing-era errors.

Foreclosures already underway when the bill passed had to be suspended and deadlines tolled, and no sale or judgment could proceed until the company complied; a sale in violation is void, and noncompliance is a bar to foreclosure under state law.

The bill banned modification fees and most foreclosure-related fees not written into the original mortgage, limited delinquency, valuation, and title-search fees, and imposed a $6,000 penalty per improper fee charged by the consumer protection bureau.

HUD would make competitive grants to states and localities for free foreclosure mediation programs requiring a decision-empowered mortgage company representative to attend, with a stay on the foreclosure until the mediator certifies good-faith compliance.
The Treasury would transfer $1 billion from proceeds of warrants sold under the 2008 bank bailout law to the Housing Trust Fund for affordable housing.

analysis.who_pays: Mortgage lenders, servicers, and the investors holding securitized mortgages would bear the cost of reworking modification protocols, producing documentation for every foreclosure, principal-reduction write-downs where modification beats foreclosure, fee limits, and mediation costs not shift-able to borrowers. Some costs could trickle into mortgage pricing, and the $1 billion Housing Trust Fund transfer would come from Treasury warrant proceeds otherwise available.

drawbacks.text: Requiring best-efforts modification reviews, full documentation, and certification before every foreclosure sale would slow foreclosures considerably and raise servicing costs, which servicers could pass along through mortgage pricing or fees elsewhere.

The bill's own text acknowledges that pooling and servicing agreements may prohibit modifications, and it mandates maximum principal reduction where modification outperforms foreclosure — a requirement that could put servicers in conflict with securitization investors and invite litigation.
The $1 billion comes from Emergency Economic Stabilization Act warrant proceeds, and the mediation grants require a 50 percent state or local match, capping how far federal dollars go.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For homeowners in the post-crisis foreclosure wave, the benefits were substantial and concrete: a documented path to a modification where that saved the mortgage holder money, proof of who holds the loan, fee limits, and free mediation. The main honest objections are that the compliance burden on servicers would slow the housing market's working-out of bad loans and that some costs would be passed to borrowers generally. On balance the design targets the well-documented robo-signing and modification-denial abuses of the era rather than blocking legitimate foreclosures outright.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in April 2011, referred to the Financial Services Committee and then to two of its subcommittees, and nothing further ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Elijah Cummings introduced the bill on April 12, 2011, joined by 23 original cosponsors, all Democrats.

It was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day, and on May 2, 2011, referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit and the Subcommittee on Insurance, Housing and Community Opportunity.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote is recorded; the action history ends with the subcommittee referrals, and the 112th Congress ended January 3, 2013.
The bill drew 51 cosponsors over its lifetime, every one of them a Democrat, and no Republican support.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Mortgage lenders, servicers, and securitization investors are better off because the bill died: they never faced mandatory modification evaluations, disclosure of foreclosure paperwork, principal-reduction requirements, fee limits, or voided sales. Homeowners facing foreclosure gained nothing from the protections it would have provided.

for.name: Rep. Elijah E. Cummings
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 23 original cosponsors from the Democratic caucus.

for.name: 51 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican cosponsored it.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Spencer Bachus, R-AL)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, passed it to two subcommittees on May 2, 2011, and never held a hearing or markup or reported it out.

sides.party_line_note: All 52 supporters — the sponsor and 51 cosponsors — were Democrats, with no Republican cosponsor, and the Republican-controlled Financial Services Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have forced them to evaluate and offer modifications that beat foreclosure on net-present-value terms, disclose origination and servicing documents, cap fees, and face voided sales for violations. Servicers' revenue from foreclosure fees and their discretion to deny modifications would have been curtailed.

The bill targeted pooling and servicing agreements believed to prohibit modifications and required maximum principal reduction where that beats foreclosure, reducing recoveries for holders of securitized mortgage debt.

industries.industry: State and local governments and housing nonprofits
industries.note: Grants for foreclosure mediation programs and a $1 billion transfer to the Housing Trust Fund would have funded new local programs and affordable housing, though grants require a 50 percent local match.
